items.title: The Green Book and the five case model
items.source: HM Treasury, The Green Book: Central Government Guidance on Appraisal and Evaluation
items.body: The Green Book is HM Treasury's guidance on how to appraise and evaluate proposals before public money is committed. It asks for a business case built from five cases. The strategic case shows why change is needed and how it fits wider goals. The economic case shows which option gives the best public value. The commercial case shows whether a workable deal can be struck with the market. The financial case shows whether the cost is affordable. The management case shows how the work will be delivered and who is accountable. A business case starts from the problem and the objectives, never from a favoured answer. Choosing the solution first and writing the case afterwards is one of the most common reasons public projects go wrong.

questions.prompt: Which HM Treasury guidance sets out how UK government appraises proposals before spending public money?

options.text: The Green Book
The Magenta Book
The Orange Book
Erskine May

questions.prompt: Which list names the five cases of a Green Book business case?

options.text: Strategic, legal, commercial, financial, delivery
Strategic, economic, commercial, financial, management
Political, economic, social, technical, legal
Policy, technical, procurement, budget, review

questions.prompt: Which case answers the question 'Is there a compelling case for change, and does it fit wider strategy?'

options.text: The economic case
The commercial case
The strategic case
The management case

questions.prompt: A team has already chosen a preferred system and now asks you to 'write the business case for it'. Explain what is wrong with this and what you would do.
questions.answer: Starting from the answer makes the case a justification instead of an appraisal. Go back to the problem and objectives, set out a long list of options including doing nothing or the minimum, shortlist against agreed criteria, compare costs, benefits and risks, and only then name a preferred option. Ask someone independent to challenge the assumptions.
questions.rubric: Must say the case should start from the case for change and objectives, not the solution. Should include a long list/shortlist with a do-nothing or do-minimum baseline, comparison on cost, benefit and risk, and independent challenge. Credit mention of bias towards a preferred answer.

items.title: Options, costs and optimism bias
items.source: HM Treasury, The Green Book: Central Government Guidance on Appraisal and Evaluation
items.body: An options appraisal compares realistic ways to meet the objectives. It always includes a baseline, often called 'do nothing' or 'business as usual', so every option can be measured against what would happen anyway. Costs and benefits that fall in different years are discounted to a present value, because a benefit now is worth more than the same benefit later. Adding them up gives a net present value. Appraisers also tend to be too hopeful about cost, time and benefits, which the Green Book calls optimism bias, so estimates are adjusted upwards and tested. The option with the highest net present value is not always chosen: benefits that cannot be priced, risks, who gains and who loses, affordability and deliverability all count.

questions.prompt: What is the 'do nothing' or 'business as usual' option for?

options.text: It is the cheapest option and is always chosen
It shows that the department has done no work
It replaces the need for a preferred option
It is the baseline every other option is compared against

questions.prompt: What is optimism bias in an appraisal?

options.text: A tendency to underestimate costs and time and overestimate benefits
A rule that benefits must be doubled
A method for pricing risk in contracts
A way of ranking options by popularity

questions.prompt: Why are costs and benefits discounted in an appraisal?

options.text: To remove inflation from the budget
So amounts that arise in different years can be compared as present values
To add a contingency for risk
To show the supplier's discount

questions.prompt: Explain what net present value is and why an option with a lower net present value might still be preferred.
questions.answer: Net present value is the total of discounted benefits minus the total of discounted costs over the appraisal period. A lower value can still win when important benefits cannot be priced, when the risk is lower, when it is more deliverable or affordable, when it is fairer in who gains, or when it fits strategy better. The reasons must be written down.
questions.rubric: Needs a correct description of NPV (discounted benefits minus costs). Should give at least two reasons a lower-NPV option may be chosen: unmonetised benefits, risk, affordability, deliverability, distribution, strategic fit. Credit for saying the reasoning is recorded.

items.title: Benefits, value for money and affordability
items.source: HM Treasury, The Green Book: Central Government Guidance on Appraisal and Evaluation
items.body: Benefits are the improvements the spending is meant to buy. A cashable benefit frees money that can be taken back into a budget; a non-cashable benefit, such as staff time freed for other work, improves the service but leaves the budget unchanged. Value for money is the best combination of whole-life cost and quality, not simply the lowest price. Whole-life cost covers buying or building, running, maintaining and finally disposing of something. Affordability is a separate test: an option can be good value and still not fit the budget available. A benefit nobody owns is unlikely to arrive, so each one needs a measure, a baseline, an owner and a date.

options.text: Any benefit that is measured in money terms
A benefit that arrives in the first year
A saving or income that can be taken back into the budget
Staff time freed up for other work

questions.prompt: Which statement about value for money is correct?

options.text: It always means the cheapest bid
It only matters for projects over £1 million
It is judged only after the service closes
It is the best mix of whole-life cost and quality, not the lowest price
Buying or building, running, maintaining and disposing of the asset or service
Only the purchase price
Only the running costs after launch
Only the costs paid in the first year

questions.prompt: A business case claims £2 million of efficiency savings, but no one owns the saving and next year's budgets are unchanged. What is the problem and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: The saving is not real until someone is accountable for it and the budget reflects it. Classify it as cashable or non-cashable, set a baseline and a measure, name an owner, profile it by year, agree the budget change with finance, and track it in benefits reporting.
questions.rubric: Should say benefits need an owner, baseline, measure and timing, and that cashable savings must change a budget. Credit for distinguishing cashable from non-cashable and for tracking realisation after approval.

items.title: Approving and reviewing the case
items.source: HM Treasury, The Green Book: Central Government Guidance on Appraisal and Evaluation
items.body: Business cases are developed in stages. A Strategic Outline Case confirms the need and the broad route. An Outline Business Case compares options and names a preferred way forward. A Full Business Case is approved when the deal is negotiated and the costs, risks and plans are firm, normally just before the main commitment is made. The case is not finished at approval. It is a living document that is revisited when cost, scope, benefits or risks change, so decision makers can see whether the work is still worth doing. After delivery, evaluation compares what happened with what the case promised, and the lessons feed the next appraisal.

questions.prompt: In the Green Book's staged approach, which is the usual order of business case documents?

options.text: Full Business Case, Outline Business Case, Strategic Outline Case
Strategic Outline Case, Outline Business Case, Full Business Case
Outline Business Case, Strategic Outline Case, Full Business Case
Strategic Outline Case, Full Business Case, Outline Business Case

questions.prompt: When is a Full Business Case normally approved?

options.text: Before anyone has defined the problem
After the service has closed
When the deal is settled, before the main contract or commitment is signed
Only once a year with the budget

questions.prompt: Why revisit the business case while the work is under way?

options.text: Because the first version is never approved
To give the project team more budget
Only if the supplier asks
Costs, scope, benefits or risks may have changed, so the work needs checking as still worthwhile

questions.prompt: What should an evaluation after delivery look at, and who should see it?
questions.answer: It compares outcomes with the objectives and benefits promised in the case, what the work cost against forecast, what worked and why, and what should change. It is shared with the sponsor, finance, assurance and the people planning similar work so lessons are used.
questions.rubric: Should cover outcomes versus objectives, benefits and costs versus the case, causes (what worked and why), and lessons. Should say the findings are shared with sponsor/board and feed future appraisals.
